title: Do Auctioneers Pick Optimal Reserve Prices?

studies.study_name: Second-price sealed-bid auction with Cuberoot distribution and variable bidder counts

findings.main_hypothesis: The optimal reserve price should not depend on the number of participating bidders (under risk neutrality). However, sellers systematically increase reserve prices as the number of bidders grows.

statistical_tests.statistical_hypothesis: Positive coefficient on the number of bidders minus the average number of bidders (n - mean(n)) in a regression of the observed reserve price in a period, with random effects for individual subjects
statistical_tests.reported_statistics: Model (1): coefficient on n - mean(n) = 2.98 [SE 0.08], p < 0.01
statistical_tests.location: Table 2, Model (1), printed page 182; model and coefficient described on page 181
statistical_tests.dependent_variable: observed reserve price in a period (page 181)
statistical_tests.coefficient_interpretation: "on average, sellers in the Cuberoot treatment increase the reservation price by 2.98 for each additional bidder" (page 181)
statistical_tests.p_value_note: Table 2 marks the coefficient with an asterisk that the table note defines as p < 0.01. No exact p-value is printed and none is derived.
statistical_tests.sample: NoInfo treatments (Table 1, page 181): Cuberoot and Cube pooled with a Cube indicator, bidder sets n in {1, 2, 3, 4} and n in {1, 4, 7, 10}, 20 seller subjects per cell (80 subjects), 60 decisions each
statistical_tests.other_models_not_scored: Model (2) adds #B - mean(#B) and keeps 2.98 [0.08]. Model (3) adds (n - mean(n)) x Cube and prints 3.24 [0.11] on n - mean(n) and -0.55 [0.15] on the interaction. The paper calls Model (1) the baseline model and interprets its 2.98 (page 181); that is the scored value.

original_data_points.description: Legacy expert-supplied human benchmark aggregates, attributed in the existing record to the University of Michigan replication. Values are preserved; provenance below distinguishes exact printed evidence, mismatches, lower-precision figures and unverified values. They are not all original-2011 paper results.

value.statistical_hypothesis: Positive coefficient on number of bidders in a regression of reserve price on bidder count
value.reported_statistics: coefficient on n = 2.98, p < .001 (original); Pearson r = 0.42, p < .001

legacy_statistical_test.reason: Mixed the original regression with a later Pearson statistic; both p < .001 claims are unsupported by the printed tables. Davis Table 2 marks p < 0.01; Feng Table 2 prints no p-value for r.

scoring.summary: Scored against Davis et al. (2011) only: Table 2 Model (1), random-effects regression of reserve price on n - mean(n), coefficient 2.98 [SE 0.08], p < 0.01. The agent decisions are fitted with the same dependent variable, the same bidder-count predictor and a random intercept per agent.

agent_model.description: Random-intercept GLS regression (Swamy-Arora variance components) of reserve price on n - mean(n) and period - mean(period), random effect per agent; conventional standard errors, two-sided z-test
agent_model.dependent_variable: agent reserve price in a round (integer 0-100)
agent_model.random_effects: agent (one simulated seller per individual_data entry)
differences_from_davis2011: No Cube indicator: the agent task replays only the Cuberoot distribution, so Cube is constant and is dropped.
Bidder set: the agent sees n in {1, 4, 7, 10} only; Davis Model (1) pools the n in {1, 2, 3, 4} and n in {1, 4, 7, 10} sets and both distributions.
n and period are centered on the agent sample's own means; centering does not change the slope.
Davis does not name the random-effects estimator; the evaluator uses the Swamy-Arora GLS estimator (the default random-effects estimator in Stata's xtreg). The Hausman test of footnote 5 is not run.
The model is not estimated with fewer than 4 agents (2 slopes + intercept need at least K + 2 subjects for the between-subject variance).

scoring.replication_rule: replication = human_significant (Davis Table 2 bound p < 0.01 <= 0.05) and the agent coefficient on n - mean(n) is significant at 0.05 and positive, the sign of the printed 2.98.
scoring.effect_comparison: agent coefficient on n - mean(n) (computed) vs the printed 2.98, both in reserve-price points per additional bidder; effect_gap = agent - 2.98.
scoring.not_used: Feng et al. (2025) is a later benchmark, kept only as a reference (see later_benchmark_see_also). Its Pearson r = 0.42 is not used in scoring.

later_benchmark_see_also.note: Later human benchmark (40 human profiles, Feng et al. 2025 Figure 1A) reported for reference only. No p-value is printed for r, and none is inferred.

original_paper_descriptives.location: Figure 2(a) NoInfo, Cuberoot bars, printed page 182
original_paper_descriptives.note: Bar labels as printed, one decimal place. The figure does not say whether n = 1 and n = 4 pool the two bidder sets. Not used in scoring.

source_set.decision: The study follows one paper, Davis et al. (2011): it alone supplies the scored human result. feng2025 is declared only because some retained legacy aggregates are printed there (see value_provenance) and as a later benchmark for reference; it is not used in scoring. Davis et al. (2023) is cited by Feng but its paper and data were not inspected.
source_set.extraction_scoring_rule: Score an item only when its provenance has printed_in containing a supplied source_id, or a fully stated derivation using supplied sources. Legacy unverified/mismatched values are not paper-extraction targets.

The figure label is the evidence, and it describes the human benchmark the later paper compares against. It is not the 2011 sample: Davis et al. (2011) Table 1 (p. 181) prints 120 seller subjects in total, 20 per treatment cell, and the text (p. 183) refers to "each of the 120 participants".
60 rounds printed for task design; does not prove replication sample size.
